question.text: Under SEBI Mutual Fund regulations, when an AMC proposes a change in the fundamental attributes of an existing scheme, which of the following protections is the AMC required to provide to existing unitholders?

answer.text: The AMC can implement the change at its discretion without giving unitholders any notice or exit option
Only SEBI approval is required; no notice or exit option needs to be given to unitholders
The AMC must give written communication to each unitholder and offer a 30-day exit option with no exit load
A simple majority vote of unitholders present at a meeting is sufficient

explanation.text: The Logic: Page 102 of the NISM Series V-A workbook states that when there is a change in the fundamental attributes of an existing scheme, the AMC must send written communication to each unitholder, and unitholders who do not wish to continue must be offered an exit option (a window of at least 30 days) without any exit load. This is the directly source-supported investor-protection mechanism. The Trap: Options A and B understate the AMC's obligations — the AMC cannot make a fundamental change unilaterally or with regulator-only approval. Option D is a corporate-style shareholder-vote mechanism that does not apply to mutual fund unitholders for fundamental-attribute changes; the regulation uses an "exit option" rather than a vote. In the audit-flagged original wording (scheme merger), candidates could argue both "exit option" and a vote because the exact merger-of-two-schemes process was not visible on the pages cited. Note: The original stem asked about the "merger of two mutual fund schemes within the same AMC", but the exact merger-process language was not found on the cited pages — only the related, source-supported "change in fundamental attributes" rule on p.102. The stem has been retargeted to the change-in-fundamental-attributes rule, which is directly supported, so the keyed exit-option answer is now unambiguous. Source: NISM Series V-A workbook, p.102.
